channel.title: Muhammad Jahanzaib Awan — Writing
channel.description: Short technical posts on machine learning, evaluation and data science.

item.title: Prompt Engineering Salary Claims: What the Job Actually Pays For
item.description: The eye-catching prompt engineer salary figures are really paying for evaluation, debugging and systems judgement, not magic phrasing.

item.title: Common ML Algorithms Grouped by the Problem They Solve
item.description: A practical map of machine learning methods organised by the underlying problem they solve, not by buzzword or library.

item.title: Prompt Engineering: What Survives a Model Change
item.description: A practical look at which prompting habits transfer across model versions, and which were just quirky workarounds that quietly stop working.

item.title: What a Model Learns During Training, on One Example
item.description: A worked example showing exactly what changes, step by step, when a model trains, with no hand-waving about magic.

item.title: RAG as Context Engineering: Where the Boundary Sits
item.description: RAG succeeds or fails on context engineering, not retrieval cleverness. Here is where the real boundary sits, and how to test it honestly.

item.title: Choosing a Deep Learning Book in a Crowded Field
item.description: Most deep learning books fail not because they are wrong but because they are read at the wrong stage. Here is how to pick one that actually moves you forward.

item.title: Deep Learning Versus Classical Statistics: The Real Overlap
item.description: Deep learning and classical statistics are often framed as rivals, but underneath the tooling they share the same core questions about bias, variance, and generalisation.

item.title: Machine Learning Engineer Titles: What the Posting Really Wants
item.description: Same title, different job. Here is how to decode what a machine learning engineer posting is actually asking for before you apply.

item.title: Context Windows Are Not the Same as Context Engineering
item.description: Bigger context windows do not fix bad retrieval. Here is why feeding a model the right information matters more than feeding it more.

item.title: Prompt Engineering Certifications: What They Actually Certify
item.description: Most prompt engineering certificates test recall of technique names, not the measurable skill of improving outputs under real constraints.

item.title: Why 'Fine-Tuning' Means Three Different Things
item.description: Fine-tuning can mean full retraining, LoRA-style adaptation, or just prompt steering. Mixing them up wastes compute and muddles your evaluation.

item.title: Fine-Tuning in Cosmology and ML: One Word, Two Claims
item.description: The word 'fine-tuning' means something precise in cosmology and something else entirely in ML. Mixing them up leads to sloppy arguments on both sides.

item.title: Deep Learning Textbooks Compared: Goodfellow Revisited
item.description: Transformers aside, the Deep Learning textbook still explains the foundations, regularisation, and optimisation better than most modern alternatives.

item.title: Machine Learning Definitions Compared: The Quiet Disagreements
item.description: Textbooks all quote similar definitions of machine learning, but look closely and they disagree on what counts as learning, generalisation, and experience.

item.title: What Genetic Perturbation Models Teach Us About Deep Learning
item.description: Models that predict cellular response to gene perturbations look impressive until you check the splits. The lessons generalise far beyond biology.

item.title: Context Engineering Versus Prompt Engineering: What Changed
item.description: Prompt wording still matters, but the real leverage moved to what you retrieve, structure, and feed a model before it answers.

item.title: Choosing a First NLP Project That Actually Teaches You Something
item.description: Skip the chatbot clone. A simple classifier, built with care, teaches tokenisation, embeddings, and evaluation far better.

item.title: What a Fine-Tuning Run Actually Costs
item.description: GPU hours are the visible cost of fine-tuning. Data curation and honest evaluation are the invisible costs that decide whether the run was worth it.

item.title: Evaluating a Model Against Its Own Baseline, Not Just the Leaderboard
item.description: Beating the leaderboard means little if your model cannot beat a trivial baseline built from its own inputs. Here is why that comparison matters.

item.title: Why Computer Vision and ML Engineers Read Papers Differently
item.description: Computer vision and general ML engineers scan the same paper for different red flags, shaped by different failure modes they have each been burned by.
